title: 2FA backup codes are kept as unsalted, unkeyed SHA-256 of a ~39.6-bit code (hardening: recoverable offline from a plain users.json copy)
description: newBackupCodes builds each code from two groups of 4 symbols of a 31-symbol alphabet (31^8 = 8.5e11, 39.6 bits) and stores sha256(code) with no salt or key in users.json. In a local in-process run (repeated), a stored hash equalled plain sha256(code), a backup made without BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY was a plain zip containing users.json (all 10 hashes) and no secret.key, and the TOTP secret in the same file was sealed. docs/security.md says the 2FA secret is sealed with secret.key and 'ส่วนรหัสสำรองเก็บเฉพาะค่าแฮช' (backup codes are kept only as hashes), and that secret.key stays out of backups; the observed result matches those statements and does not contradict them. The weakness is that the hash is fast and unsalted, so a holder of a users.json copy could in principle search the code space offline (arithmetic only, not run: 8.5e11 at about 1.1-1.8M hashes/s measured is about 5-9 days on one core, less with 10 targets). The attacker would also need the account password (argon2id), and online guessing is locked out. No request hands such a copy to a low-trust caller (download route is admin-only). This is a defence-in-depth hardening note with no crossed boundary demonstrated.
root_cause: Backup codes are a low-entropy secret protected by a fast unkeyed hash (createHash sha256, no salt, no pepper, no secret.key HMAC) while the TOTP secret beside it is sealed with secret.key.
intended_behavior: docs/security.md: the 2FA secret is sealed with secret.key (kept out of backups) and backup codes are stored only as hashes. Not stated in the docs: that the hashes must resist offline search; this is a hardening expectation.

trace.description: admin-only route (requireAdmin at line 54) by which a plain backup containing users.json leaves the server; the same file is also in any copy of DATA_DIR or the backup folder, which is outside the request surface
hashes: codes.map(sha256), unsalted and unkeyed; stored in user.twoFactor.backup at line 376 and written to users.json
a backup code whose sha256 is in tf.backup is accepted as the second factor and then removed

evidence.description: BACKUP_ALPHABET has 31 symbols; the code is 4+4 characters
sha256 helper: createHash('sha256').update(s).digest('hex'), no salt or key
SKIP list keeps secret.key out of the backup but users.json (with the backup-code hashes) is included

conditions.description: Attacker holds a copy of users.json or a backup made without BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY (stolen volume, off-site copy, leaked backup file); no app request provides this to a low-trust caller
Target account has 2FA enabled and has unused backup codes; attacker also needs the account password (argon2id hash in the same file) to reach the second step

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of an unencrypted backup zip or users.json copy, offline.
payloads: sha256 of every candidate xxxx-xxxx over alphabet abcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz23456789, compared against twoFactor.backup in users.json
instructions: Create a 2FA user in an in-process app with a sandboxed STORAGE_DIR and DATA_DIR and no BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY
Call runBackup and list the zip: users.json present, secret.key absent
Read users.json from the zip: twoFactor.backup hashes equal sha256 of the plain codes; twoFactor.secret is sealed
Time 2M SHA-256 hashes locally for the rate; compute 31^8 / rate as arithmetic
execution.observed_result: Repeated runs: hash == sha256(code) true; zip contains users.json and no secret.key; all 10 hashes in the zip equal sha256 of the codes; TOTP secret sealed; 1.1-1.8M hashes/s. Full-space search time is arithmetic, not run; no code was actually recovered.

remediation.strategy: Store the backup codes as an HMAC keyed with a secret derived from secret.key (which is kept out of backups), or as slow salted hashes (argon2id) per code, or lengthen the code so offline search is impractical; compare in constant time.

likelihood.reason: needs a plain backup or users.json copy first (outside the request surface), plus the account password

impact.reason: demonstrated result matches the documented design (hashes only, TOTP secret sealed); the recovery of a code is arithmetic, not demonstrated, and costs days of compute

confidence.reason: hash, backup contents and sealed TOTP secret were observed in repeated local runs and re-run by the final verifier; the search time is only arithmetic

title: Anonymous guest or share-link holder can rotate earlier audit entries away with repeated downloads
description: Every successful non-inline GET /api/download (guest allowed by default guestPermissions on the public space) and every GET /api/s/:token/download writes one audit line with no dedupe, rate limit or per-caller cap, whereas failed sign-ins (session.ts:70) and browse use deduplication so they cannot fill and rotate away the trail. In a bounded in-process run with the audit cap lowered to 4096 bytes x 2 files (the real cap is a code literal, not configurable), an anonymous session repeated GET /api/download of one 5-byte public file: all 600 requests returned 200 and an earlier admin entry (user creation) was gone from audit.log and audit.log.1 after request 71. The same happened through an unlimited share link (600/600 200, admin entry gone). Measured line sizes: 113 bytes (guest download, in-process ip 'unknown') and 163 bytes (share download). Arithmetic, not measured at scale: the default 10 x 10 MiB = 104,857,600 bytes would take about 928,000 guest downloads (104857600/113) or about 643,000 share downloads (104857600/163); real client IPs make lines slightly longer, so somewhat fewer. The forwarding queue was not exercised (no forwarding configured; source: audit-forward.ts:80 drops the newest entries at 1000 queued), so the SIEM copy claim is source-only. The cost is large, the flood is itself visible until it overwrites, and a configured SIEM keeps its already-forwarded copy, so impact is bounded.
root_cause: audit() is called on every public download path without the auditOnce/auditFailure dedupe or any per-caller cap, and rotateFile unlinks the oldest file once maxFiles is reached, so the capacity of the trail is controlled by unauthenticated request volume.
intended_behavior: A principal with no account must not be able to push earlier audit entries out of the trail; high-volume anonymous events should be deduplicated or aggregated per key and window as failed sign-ins are (session.ts:70-71).

trace.description: audit() on every non-inline download; user null becomes 'guest'. The share-link route (src/routes/shares.ts:328, GET /api/s/:token/download, no login, no limit when maxDownloads is null) reaches the same audit() and is a second propagation path.
appendLine to audit.log with auditMaxBytes/auditMaxFiles, then forwardAudit; no dedupe
unlinkSync of the oldest rotated file once all maxFiles are used, so older entries are lost

evidence.description: audit() per download, guest user label, no dedupe
audit() per share download inside startDownload slot, no dedupe
auditMaxBytes 10 MiB and auditMaxFiles 10 are literals (lowered only in the test by mutating config)
comment states the invariant for failed sign-ins: must not be able to fill and rotate away the trail
queue bounded at maxQueue, newest dropped (source-only, not run)

No reverse proxy or tunnel rate limit; at default caps roughly 0.6 to 0.9 million requests are needed (arithmetic from measured line sizes)

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous visitor with only the public page, or a holder of one unlimited share link
instructions: Boot the app in-process with fresh dirs, record an admin action (create user) in the audit log
Lower config.auditMaxBytes to 4096 and auditMaxFiles to 2 in-process
As an anonymous session repeat the public download 600 times, then do the same through an unlimited share link
Search audit.log and audit.log.1 for the admin entry
execution.observed_result: 600/600 downloads 200, no dedupe or rate limit intervened, admin entry gone from audit.log and audit.log.1 (after request 71 for guest download; also gone after the share-link flood); run twice, identical.

remediation.strategy: Deduplicate anonymous and share downloads with auditOnce keyed per (ip or share id, target) per minute with a repeat count, or add a per-caller cap; optionally keep a separate non-rotating store for administrative actions.

likelihood.reason: Needs roughly 0.6 to 0.9 million requests at default caps (arithmetic), reachable anonymously but noisy and subject to any proxy rate limit.

impact.reason: Audit trail integrity is a protected asset and an account-less principal erases earlier admin entries, but only a bounded history window and not other data or access.

confidence.reason: Mechanism reproduced end to end with a lowered in-process cap; default-scale arithmetic and the forwarding drop were not run.

title: POST /api/batch retains one token entry per call with no cap, reachable by an anonymous visitor in the default configuration
description: Each POST /api/batch stores {owner, space, root, dir, names[], expires} in the module-level Map batches for 5 minutes. The only removal is the expiry sweep on the next POST; there is no per-session, per-address or global cap. In an in-process run in the sandbox, an anonymous session with its CSRF token called POST /api/batch 2000 times on a public folder of 300 files (name length about 55 chars), naming all files. All 2000 calls returned 200 with a token, and the first and the last token were still redeemable (GET /api/batch/:token gave 200). Heap grew by about 82.8 MB (about 42 KB per entry, about 140 bytes per name) in about 1.3 to 1.6 s of handler time (about 1 ms per call, so the O(n) sweep was not a limiter at this size). No app-level rate limit was found on this route. Arithmetic, not measured: at the same per-call cost, 100000 calls would hold about 4 GB for 5 minutes, and a folder near the 2000-name per-request limit would hold about 280 KB per entry. Real HTTP overhead and any proxy rate limit or container memory limit would change the rate; those are deployment facts that were not observed. No saturation was run.
root_cause: The batches Map has time-based expiry only; there is no cardinality or per-principal bound, and each entry stores the full name list.
intended_behavior: Batch tokens should be bounded like the other visitor-reachable maps (anonymous sessions 5000, auditOnce 5000, attempts 10000): cap total and per-owner entries, or evict the oldest, or encode the selection in a signed token instead of server memory.

trace.description: need(space, download, batchdownload) passes for an anonymous session on the public space with default guestPermissions

batches.set(token, {... names ...}) with no size check

conditions.description: Anonymous session plus its CSRF token (GET /api/session); no login
Public page on (default) and guestPermissions include download and batchdownload (default)
The public folder holds at least one file; entry size scales with the number of names (up to 2000 per call)
A rate limit in a reverse proxy or tunnel and the container memory limit were not observed and decide how fast it grows

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous visitor with a session cookie and CSRF token, calling the batch endpoint repeatedly
payloads: POST /api/batch {"space":"public","path":"/","items":["<all 300 existing file names>"]} repeated 2000 times
instructions: GET /api/session, keep the fc_sid cookie and csrf

execution.observed_result: 2000 of 2000 calls returned 200; first and last token redeemable with 200; heap grew about 82.8 MB (about 42 KB per entry) in two runs (82816 and 82820 KB); about 1 ms per call.

remediation.strategy: Cap the Map (global and per owner, evicting the oldest or refusing with 429 when full), and sweep on a timer; or make the token self-contained and signed so that no server memory is held.

likelihood.reason: Reachable without login in the default configuration with one session and CSRF token; cost to the caller is one small request per entry. A proxy rate limit may slow it.

impact.reason: Memory is retained for 5 minutes per entry and grows linearly: about 4 GB at 100000 calls (arithmetic). The shared single Bun process is affected, but no exhaustion was demonstrated and the effect clears after expiry or restart.

confidence.reason: Retention and per-entry size were measured twice in-process; the exhaustion point, HTTP-level request rate and deployment limits were not measured.

title: A restored older account reads the activity of a later same-name account through /api/me/activity and /api/me/export
description: ownEntries keeps audit entries with r.user === username and ts >= createdAt of the account, a lower time bound only. After alice#1 is deleted and alice#2 is created, a restore of a backup taken while alice#1 existed brings alice#1 back with its older createdAt (users.json is swapped, planRestore drops the live instance's records). restoreBackup rewrites only users, settings and branding; logs/audit.log is not touched (not extracted, kept). End to end run in the sandbox: after the restore and restart, alice#1 signs in with the old password and GET /api/me/activity returns alice#2's login and app-password-create entries (target SECOND-ALICE-SECRET-DEVICE). POST /api/me/export uses the same filter (my-data.ts:58). The delete and the re-create do not bound or rewrite the log either. Restore was driven by calling restoreBackup (the function the route calls) in a child process, then a fresh process for the check, as tests/security-1132-restore.test.ts does; the HTTP restore route itself was not run. The export path was read in source, not run.
root_cause: src/my-data.ts ownEntries (line 48) approximates the account instance by a lower time bound on createdAt; audit entries carry no instance id and nothing bounds the end of an earlier instance's life, and the restore leaves the audit log as it is.
intended_behavior: An account sees only entries it wrote itself; an earlier or later account of the same name is another person (my-data.ts header lines 37-42, and the account instance rule (name, createdAt) used for sessions, shares, grants and app passwords).

LOGS_KEPT: logs are kept in place, not part of a restore

title: A LINE link code issued by a deleted account still links a LINE user to a new account of the same name
description: issueLinkCode (POST /api/me/line/link) keeps { username, expires } in a memory map for ten minutes. forgetAccount, called by DELETE /api/admin/users/:username and by POST /api/admin/users, does not clear that map. A former holder who generated a code while the account existed can, if an admin deletes and re-creates that username within ten minutes, send the code to the LINE bot from their own LINE account. The signed webhook handler redeems it to the bare username, resolves it with findUser to the NEW account and linkLine ties the sender's LINE id to it. Observed end to end in-process: the new account's notify-prefs showed line.linked false before and true after a self-signed webhook. The sender then gets that account's LINE pushes once the new owner enables the line channel for a kind (off by default per kind); the bot also replies with the new account's display name.
root_cause: src/line.ts codes map stores only the username and is never invalidated on account deletion or re-creation; src/account-records.ts forgetAccount clears every other per-account store but not this one, and redeem does not bind the code to the account instance (name, createdAt).
intended_behavior: A deleted account takes every record that names it along; a new account of the same name must not be reachable through anything the earlier one issued (account instance rule in the header of src/account-records.ts).

trace.description: forgetAccount(target.username) is the account cleanup after splice (POST /api/admin/users line 182 calls it too before pushing the new account)

title: Two concurrent admin account creations with the same username both succeed
description: POST /api/admin/users checks findUser(username) at line 166, then awaits hashPassword at line 190 inside the argument of allUsers().push(...). Two simultaneous admin requests both pass the check and both push, leaving two accounts with one name. findUser and login see only the first (second password gives 401); once the first is deleted, the hidden second becomes the live account with the password the creator chose. Correction to the candidate: the manager case does NOT reproduce. For a manager the second request is stopped with 409 admin.home-exists (homeIsTaken at line 175), because the first request creates the home directory synchronously (ensureDir line 178) before its await. Only an admin (who bypasses homeIsTaken) can hit the race. Impact: an admin can already create, delete and reset any account, so the duplicate gives no new capability beyond a hidden same-name record and a broken uniqueness invariant.
root_cause: Check-then-act across an await: uniqueness is checked at src/routes/admin.ts:166 but the push at line 185 only happens after await hashPassword at line 190; nothing re-checks findUser after the await. For managers the sync ensureDir at line 178 plus homeIsTaken at line 175 incidentally closes the window.
intended_behavior: A username has exactly one live account; a second concurrent create with the same name must get 409 admin.username-taken.

trace.description: requireStaff caller; only an admin reaches the race
findUser(username) uniqueness check before any await
await hashPassword inside the push argument (push at line 185); second request passes line 166 meanwhile and pushes a duplicate

evidence.description: only uniqueness check, runs before the await
await hashPassword(body.password) delays the push, no re-check

remediation.strategy: Hash the password before the checks, then re-run findUser (and homeIsTaken for managers) synchronously immediately before the push; or hold a per-name creating set.

impact.reason: admin already holds full account authority; result is a hidden duplicate record and a broken name-uniqueness invariant, no privilege or data gained; managers are blocked

confidence.reason: reproduced twice in the sandbox with admin (duplicate) and manager (blocked) callers

title: An admin session alone can mint a new admin with a chosen password and then pass every password step-up
description: POST /api/admin/users with role admin, and PUT /api/admin/users/:username with a password, ask an admin caller for no password. A holder of only an admin session cookie creates a second admin with a password of their choosing, signs in as it, and passes confirmPassword on step-up routes (observed: PUT /api/admin/settings with a security group returned 200 using the new admin's password and 403 with a wrong one). docs/security.md says a stolen session alone cannot change sign-in rules because the admin password is asked. The settings step-up field is body.password, not confirmPassword.
root_cause: confirmPassword is checked against the signed-in account's own hash, and the routes that mint or re-key an admin account (create with role admin, set password / promote role as admin) have no step-up, so the control can be re-derived through a new principal. src/routes/admin.ts:232 requires step-up only when the actor is not an admin.
intended_behavior: Creating an admin, promoting to admin, or setting another admin's password should need the acting admin's own password (confirmPassword), like the other sensitive admin actions, so a stolen session alone cannot obtain a password it knows.

trace.description: requireStaff at 160; an admin may pass role admin (162 refuses only non-admins); no password asked; hashes the supplied password at 190

verifies the supplied password against the signed-in account's own hash, so the attacker-made admin passes it

Login as evil2 in a second client: 200

title: In-flight upload completion survives account deletion and charges the next same-name account
description: dropUploadsOf skips uploads whose id is in the finishing set, and finishUpload does not re-check the owner after the slow antivirus gate. If an admin deletes and re-creates an account while its complete is waiting on the scan, the upload is neither dropped nor released: the file still lands in the old home and the same-name new account is charged (reservation kept, then commitBytes) by username only.
root_cause: dropUploadsOf leaves finishing uploads alone and nothing later re-validates the owner's account instance (name, createdAt) after the gate; quota reservation and commitBytes are keyed by lowercase username only.
intended_behavior: An account's unfinished uploads must not complete or be charged after the account is deleted, re-created or dropped by restore, as the comment above dropUploadsOf states.

trace.description: completeUpload is called for the account before it is deleted (the hunter cited line 54; the call is on line 53).
finishing.has(meta.id) causes the upload and its reservation to be skipped when the account is dropped.
await gate(...) is the slow step; stillAllowed (line 417) ran only before it and is not repeated.
commitBytes(meta.quotaUser, meta.size) charges whichever account currently has that name; putInPlace at line 443 already placed the file in the old home.

evidence.description: dropUploadsOf skips finishing uploads.
commit by username only after the gate, no owner re-check.

conditions.description: An admin deletes (or a restore drops) the account during the window of one complete.
The window is the clamd scan time or a slow EXDEV copy; antivirus must be on (or the copy slow).
The charge is visible only if a same-name account is re-created; the cached usage clears at the next recount.

execution.attacker_perspective: Authenticated user whose account is being deleted; the upload was authorized before deletion.
payloads: announce 3000 B, PUT chunk 0, POST complete (fake clamd answers after 1.5 s); admin DELETE /api/admin/users/victim; admin POST /api/admin/users victim with homedir /users/victim2
instructions: Run s3.ts <dir> keep in the sandbox with the fake clamd delaying its answer (antivirus enabled in settings).
execution.observed_result: Independent re-run, two identical runs: delete 200 with the upload still in tmp; the new same-name account showed 3000 bytes used before complete ended; complete returned 200 after deletion; file landed in /users/victim (old home), none in /users/victim2; usage stayed 3000 afterwards; new account got 404 on the old upload id (no takeover).

remediation.strategy: Record the account createdAt in Meta; after the gate and before commitBytes verify the owner exists with the same createdAt, otherwise drop the upload and release holds. Alternatively let dropUploadsOf mark finishing uploads cancelled so finishUpload aborts.

likelihood.reason: Needs an admin delete and re-create inside the scan window of one complete.

impact.reason: One already-authorized file written once into the dropped account's old home; transient phantom quota of at most the file size until recount.

confidence.reason: Reproduced twice in the sandbox; source lines re-read and match.

title: Central-directory entry/size pre-check bypassed by a fake EOCD hidden in the real EOCD comment
description: checkDirectory reads the last PK\5\6 signature in the file tail, while zip.js uses the EOCD that actually locates the directory. A zip whose real (ZIP64) EOCD has a 22-byte comment holding a zero-count EOCD passes the check, yet zip.js still loads the whole directory. Locally a 120000-entry zip (cap 100000) was refused 413 when plain but passed when crafted; zip.js getEntries then read 120000 entries and grew RSS by about 300 MB for a roughly 6 MB file (about 50x). The pre-check exists solely to stop zip.js holding an oversized directory in memory. After the bypass only the file size (UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE default 10 GB), the post-hoc files.length check in unzipTo (read after getEntries) and the 10000-entry display cut in listArchive (applied after the directory is loaded) remain, and none bound zip.js memory. Reached through archive list/file, unzip, and the share archive routes.
root_cause: The pre-check and the parser pick different EOCD records: the check takes the last signature in the tail, zip.js takes the one that locates a valid directory.
intended_behavior: DIRECTORY_MAX_BYTES and DIRECTORY_MAX_ENTRIES are enforced on the same EOCD record zip.js will parse, so an oversized directory is refused before zip.js reads it.

title: Unzip creates unbounded implied directories with synchronous mkdir, stalling the single server thread
description: POST /api/unzip applies maxFiles and maxBytes only to non-directory entries; the total entry count (directories included) is capped at unzipMaxFiles (50000) by checkDirectory, but the directories each deep path implies are not counted. Directory entries are created with mkdirSync recursive inside a loop with no await. A small zip of deeply nested directory entries therefore creates a very large number of inodes and blocks the shared event loop while they are made. Reproduced through the real route: a 42 KB zip of 20 entries nested 500 deep gave 200 OK, 0 files and 10,020 directories, with a longest event-loop stall of 150-233 ms (5 ms timer) across runs. Growth is linear in implied directories; larger sizes were not run.
root_cause: unzipTo caps only non-directory entries by count and bytes (src/zip.ts:182-184); the entry-total cap at line 178 counts entries, not the parent directories each name implies. The entry.directory branch (198-199) calls mkdirSync(target,{recursive:true}) with no depth or created-directory counter and no yield.
intended_behavior: Count created directories (including implied parents) and/or bound path depth toward a cap, and yield or use async mkdir so extraction does not hold the single server thread.
